meta.titre: Retail Trade: types of retailers and what they offer
meta.sous_theme: Small and large retailers, their services and mark-up

sections.contenu_markdown: To buy a notebook, a pen or a bar of soap you do not travel to a factory. You go to a kiosk, a stall in the market or a supermarket. These sellers are retailers: the last link in the chain between the producer and you. Retail trade is a regular topic in GCE Commerce because it is part of daily life and because it mixes definitions, comparisons and a little arithmetic. This course explains the types of retailers, what they offer and how a retailer fixes a selling price.

items: The chain of distribution passes from the producer to the wholesaler, to the retailer and to the consumer.
A wholesaler buys in large quantities and sells in smaller lots to retailers.
A consumer is the person who uses the goods.

sections.titre: Retailers, their types and their services
sections.contenu_markdown:
### The retailer

A **retailer** buys goods from producers or wholesalers and sells them in small quantities to the final consumer. By stocking a wide range of goods near the buyers, the retailer saves the consumer the trouble of travelling and buying in bulk.

### Services of retailers

- To consumers: goods in convenient places and in small amounts, a choice of goods, advice, and sometimes credit or home delivery.
- To wholesalers and manufacturers: **breaking bulk**, holding stock, displaying goods and passing on information about customers' tastes.

### Types of retailers

| Type | Main features |
|---|---|
| Hawker (itinerant) | Moves from place to place carrying goods; no fixed premises; low capital |
| Market stall or kiosk | A small fixed place selling a narrow range of goods |
| General shop | A small shop selling many kinds of everyday goods near homes |
| Supermarket | A large self-service shop with a wide range of goods, mainly food and household items |
| Department store | A large shop with many departments, each selling different goods, **under one roof** |
| Chain (multiple) store | A firm with **many shops in different places under one management**, selling similar goods and buying centrally |
| Mail-order or online business | Customers order from a catalogue or website; goods are delivered |
| Consumer co-operative | A shop owned by its members, who share the surplus among themselves |

### Small-scale and large-scale retailers

Small retailers are close to customers, need little capital and can serve people personally. Large retailers have more capital, buy in larger quantities and offer a wider choice.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question gives a cost price and asks for the selling price or the profit
variantes.contenu_markdown: $$\text{Mark-up} = \frac{\text{profit}}{\text{cost price}} \times 100 \qquad \text{Margin} = \frac{\text{profit}}{\text{selling price}} \times 100$$ Selling price = cost price + profit. Mark-up is based on cost; margin on selling price. For the same sale the margin is always smaller than the mark-up.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to account for the growth or survival of small retail shops
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give a factor, explain it, and relate it to the country. Examples: little capital is needed to start; they are close to homes; they sell in very small quantities; the owner knows the customers and may give credit; they can open for long hours; and many people lack the money or transport to reach large shops.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks you to distinguish between two retailers
variantes.contenu_markdown: Name one feature for each side. Example: a department store is one large shop with several departments under one roof, whereas a chain store is many shops under one management in different places.

sections.enonce_markdown: A retailer buys 60 packets of washing powder at 800 FCFA each and sells them all at a mark-up of 25%. Calculate (a) the total cost, (b) the selling price per packet, (c) the total revenue, (d) the total profit and (e) the margin.

etapes.justification: Number of packets multiplied by the cost of one.
Mark-up is a percentage of the cost, so add it to the cost.
Selling price multiplied by the number sold.
Profit divided by the selling price (the revenue), times 100.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Total cost 48,000 FCFA; selling price 1,000 FCFA; revenue 60,000 FCFA; profit 12,000 FCFA; margin 20%.** The margin (20%) is lower than the mark-up (25%) because it is calculated on the larger figure, the selling price.

items.erreur_markdown: 'A department store is a firm with many shops in different towns under one management.'
items.pourquoi_faux: That describes a chain (multiple) store. A department store is one large shop with many departments under one roof.
items.correction_markdown: Department store: many departments, one building. Chain store: many shops, one management.

items.erreur_markdown: 'A retailer sells goods in large quantities to wholesalers.'
items.pourquoi_faux: That is the work of a wholesaler. A retailer sells small quantities to final consumers.
items.correction_markdown: Retailer: small quantities to consumers. Wholesaler: large quantities to retailers.

items.erreur_markdown: Calculating mark-up on the selling price
items.pourquoi_faux: Mark-up is based on the cost price. Using the selling price gives the margin.
items.correction_markdown: Mark-up = profit / cost price × 100. Margin = profit / selling price × 100.

items.erreur_markdown: 'Hawkers have fixed shops and a large stock.'
items.pourquoi_faux: Hawkers move from place to place with a small stock and do not have fixed premises.
items.correction_markdown: Hawkers: itinerant, small stock, low capital. A shop or kiosk has a fixed place.

items.erreur_markdown: Answering a growth question with one-word reasons such as 'cheap' or 'near'
items.pourquoi_faux: The question asks for a description. A word with no explanation earns little credit.
items.correction_markdown: 'Little capital: a trader can start with a small stock, so many people can open small shops.'

items.enonce_markdown: Name the type of retailer in each case: (a) a trader who walks through the streets with goods in a basket; (b) one large shop with a furniture department, an electrical department and a clothing department; (c) a firm with twelve branches in different towns under one management.
items.solution_markdown: (a) A **hawker (itinerant retailer)**. (b) A **department store**, because the departments are under one roof. (c) A **chain (multiple) store**, because many shops are managed together.

items.enonce_markdown: A shopkeeper buys 40 items at 5,500 FCFA each and sells each at 6,600 FCFA. Calculate the total profit and the mark-up.
items.solution_markdown:
Profit per item $= 6\,600 - 5\,500 = 1\,100$ FCFA.

Total profit $= 40 \times 1\,100 = 44\,000$ FCFA.

Mark-up $= \frac{1\,100}{5\,500} \times 100 = 20\%$.

**Total profit 44,000 FCFA; mark-up 20%.**

items.enonce_markdown: Many town dwellers continue to buy from small neighbourhood shops although supermarkets exist. (a) Explain three reasons for this (6 marks). (b) State two advantages that a supermarket has over a small shop (2 marks). (c) Name one service a retailer offers to a wholesaler (1 mark).
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Any three, 2 marks each (reason and explanation): the shop is **close to homes**, saving transport costs; goods are sold in **very small quantities** to buyers with little money; the owner may give **credit** to known customers; the shop opens for **long hours**; **personal service** and trust.

(b) Any two: wider choice, lower prices from buying in large quantities, self-service, goods under one roof (1 mark each).

(c) Any one: breaking bulk, holding stock, displaying goods, passing on customers' tastes (1 mark).

items_markdown: A retailer buys from producers or wholesalers and sells small quantities to final consumers.
Small retailers: hawkers, stalls, kiosks, general shops. Large retailers: supermarkets, department stores, chain stores, mail order, co-operatives.
A department store has many departments under one roof; a chain store has many shops in different places under one management.
Retailers break bulk, hold stock and offer convenience, choice, advice and sometimes credit and delivery.
Mark-up = profit / cost price × 100; margin = profit / selling price × 100; the margin is smaller than the mark-up.
For growth or survival questions, give the factor and explain it.
